screens.title: Temporary configuration with the ip command
screens.narratorSegment: The ip command is the modern, supported tool for temporary network changes and inspection. Use it to add or remove addresses, bring interfaces up or down, and manipulate routes. These changes take effect immediately in the kernel but do not survive a reboot or a service restart. For example, when you need to validate a static address on a new subnet, you might add an address and test connectivity with ping. A concrete example is running a single ip addr add command to assign 192.168.1.100/24 to an interface and then pinging the gateway to confirm reachability. Remember the common misconception: ip changes are not permanent. If you reboot or NetworkManager overwrites the interface, your address will disappear. Another common pitfall is mistyping the interface name or the CIDR, which instantly isolates the server. Always verify with ip addr show and ip route show after changes. In practice perform temporary changes incrementally and test connectivity at each step; if the test succeeds and you intend to keep the settings, translate the same values into your persistent method rather than relying on ip to survive reboots. How will you verify a temporary address before committing it?

keyIdea.title: Temporary vs permanent
keyIdea.text: ip command changes are immediate but ephemeral; use them for tests, not as a replacement for boot-time configuration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Temporary configuration with ip
Why use ip now?

Fast changes let you test reachability and routing without writing files. Use this for troubleshooting or quick experiments.

Key commands
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
sudo ip link set enp0s3 up
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
sudo ip addr del 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
After each command, verify with:
  • ip addr show to view assigned addresses
  • ip route show to confirm default routes
Concrete example
Assign 192.168.1.100/24 to enp0s3, bring it up, then ping gateway 192.168.1.1 to verify.
Common mistake
Typos in the IP or interface name cause immediate isolation. Always double-check and confirm with ip addr show.
Key Takeaway

Use ip for quick tests, then convert the same values into your persistent configuration if they must survive a reboot.

screens.title: Adding and verifying routes
screens.narratorSegment: Routing determines how packets leave the host to reach remote networks. Adding a default route tells the kernel where to send traffic destined for addresses outside the local subnet. Use the ip route add default via command to set a gateway, then validate with ip route show. A practical example is adding default via 192.168.1.1 after configuring a static address so your host can reach the internet or other subnets. A common misconception is that assigning an IP alone always provides connectivity; without the correct gateway and route, external communication fails. To safely change routing on a remote host, add the route temporarily and test connectivity before making it persistent. If you must revert, use ip route del to remove the route. Always verify that the gateway is reachable from the local subnet with a ping or arp check before setting it as the default. How would you confirm that traffic to an external IP uses your new gateway? Use traceroute or ip route get to inspect the forwarding decision. Adding and verifying routes means a default route directs outbound traffic; add it temporarily with ip route add then verify before committing changes.. In practical terms, how to add a default route and confirm path selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Adding and verifying routes
Step-by-step
  1. Confirm interface address with ip addr show.
  2. Add the default gateway: sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1.
  3. Verify with ip route show and ip route get 8.8.8.8.
  4. Test reachability with ping or traceroute.
  5. Remove with sudo ip route del default if needed.
Verification
Use ip route get to see the chosen interface and gateway for a specific destination. This helps debug asymmetric or missing routes.
Concrete example
After assigning 192.168.1.100/24, add the default via 192.168.1.1, then run ip route get 8.8.8.8. Confirm the chosen gateway and interface before pinging.
Common mistake
Setting a gateway that is not on the local subnet prevents routing to external networks. The kernel cannot ARP for an off-subnet gateway.
Key Takeaway

Routes are as important as addresses; always verify gateway reachability before committing routing changes.

screens.title: NetworkManager: nmcli vs nmtui
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkManager is a widely used daemon that manages network connections and can persist settings across reboots. It exposes two complementary tools: nmcli, a full-featured command-line interface suitable for scripting and automation, and nmtui, a simple text-based interactive interface for quick edits. Use nmcli when you need to automate configuration or create reproducible connections; it's the tool to include in configuration scripts or infrastructure-as-code. Use nmtui when you want an approachable guided UI to edit a connection interactively without memorizing a long command. A concrete example is creating a static connection with nmcli that sets IPv4 method to manual, assigns addresses and gateway, and enables autoconnect. A common misconception is that NetworkManager always overrides manual file edits; depending on your renderer and service state, file-based edits may still be used. After creating or modifying a connection, bring it up with nmcli connection up to activate it immediately. Always verify with nmcli connection show and ip addr show. Which tool you pick depends on whether you need automation or a quick interactive fix. NetworkManager: nmcli vs nmtui means use nmcli for automation and scripting, nmtui for guided interactive edits; both persist settings via networkmanager.. In practical terms, scriptable nmcli and interactive nmtui for persistent configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › NetworkManager: nmcli vs nmtui
nmcli (scriptable)
nmcli device status
nmcli connection show
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name my-static-eth0 ifname enp0s3 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 autoconnect yes
sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0
Use nmcli in scripts and automations to ensure reproducible setup across hosts.
nmtui (interactive)
nmtui opens a curses-style interactive editor to add or edit connections. It's ideal for administrators who prefer a guided interface without memorizing options.
Concrete scenario
Create a static connection via nmcli in automation. If a colleague prefers GUI-like editing, use nmtui to verify or change DNS and autoconnect settings quickly.
Key Takeaway

Choose the tool that matches your workflow: nmcli for reproducible scripts; nmtui for guided interactive edits.

screens.title: Persistent configuration: Red Hat ifcfg files
screens.narratorSegment: On Red Hat-derived systems persistent network settings are typically stored as ifcfg files in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts. Each interface has an ifcfg- file that lists variables such as DEVICE, IPADDR, PREFIX, GATEWAY, DNS1, and ONBOOT. When NetworkManager or the network service starts, it reads these files and configures interfaces accordingly. A concrete example is creating /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-enp0s3 with IPADDR set to 192.168.1.100 and PREFIX to 24, and ONBOOT=yes to ensure it comes up at boot. After saving edits, you must restart the appropriate service, usually systemctl restart NetworkManager or systemctl restart network, to apply changes. A common misconception is that editing the file alone immediately changes the live configuration; it does not until the service re-reads the file. When working remotely, plan a rollback or console access before restarting networking. Verify the applied values with ip addr show and ip route show after the restart to confirm that the persistent file produced the expected runtime state. Persistent configuration: Red Hat ifcfg files means ifcfg scripts declare persistent network settings on rhel-family systems; editing them requires a service restart to take effect.. In practical terms, how to author an ifcfg file and apply changes on rhel-family systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Persistent configuration: ifcfg files
Example ifcfg file
TYPE=Ethernet
BOOTPROTO=none
DEFROUTE=yes
NAME=enp0s3
DEVICE=enp0s3
ONBOOT=yes
IPADDR=192.168.1.100
PREFIX=24
GATEWAY=192.168.1.1
DNS1=8.8.8.8
After editing, restart NetworkManager or the network service to apply the settings.
Apply and verify
  • Restart: sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager or sudo systemctl restart network
  • Verify runtime state with ip addr show and ip route show.
Common mistake
Editing ifcfg without restarting the service leaves runtime unchanged. Do not rely on file edits alone to reconfigure a live interface.
Key Takeaway

Ifcfg files control persistent settings on RHEL systems; always restart and verify after edits, and plan for rollback on remote hosts.

screens.title: Netplan on Ubuntu/Debian
screens.narratorSegment: Netplan provides a YAML-based abstraction for network configuration on Ubuntu and some Debian systems. Instead of editing multiple legacy files, you author a YAML file under /etc/netplan that describes interfaces, addresses, gateway, and nameservers, and specify a renderer such as networkd or NetworkManager. After saving your YAML, run netplan apply to translate the configuration into the system's backend and apply it immediately. A concrete example is defining enp0s3 with dhcp4 set to no, addresses to 192.168.1.100/24, gateway4 to 192.168.1.1, and nameservers with 8.8.8.8. A common misconception is that YAML indentation is forgiving; it is strict, and a formatting error prevents netplan from applying. Always validate changes and keep a console access plan when modifying network configuration remotely. Use netplan try on systems that support it; it provides a rollback timer if connectivity is lost. After a successful apply, verify runtime state with ip addr show and ip route show. Netplan on Ubuntu/Debian means netplan yaml describes desired state and is applied to the system's renderer; indentation and syntax must be correct to avoid failures.. In practical terms, author netplan yaml and apply networkd or networkmanager renderers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Netplan on Ubuntu/Debian
Example Netplan YAML
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp0s3:
      dhcp4: no
      addresses: [192.168.1.100/24]
      gateway4: 192.168.1.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4]
Apply with sudo netplan apply. Use netplan try where available for a reversible test.
Practical advice
  • Keep indentation exact; YAML is sensitive to whitespace.
  • Prefer netplan try when changing remote server settings to avoid lockout.
  • Verify with ip addr show and ip route show after applying.
Common mistake
Incorrect YAML syntax prevents netplan from applying and may leave the interface unchanged. Always validate syntax and use a safe apply procedure.
Key Takeaway

Netplan centralizes network configuration with a clear YAML format; apply carefully and verify changes to avoid losing remote access.

screens.title: Safe workflow for editing network config on remote servers
screens.narratorSegment: Modifying network settings on a remote server carries risk: a misconfigured interface can cut your access. Adopt a safe workflow: first, discover the current state with ip addr show and ip route show; second, plan changes and craft them as either temporary ip commands or persistent file edits; third, test changes temporarily so you can confirm connectivity. If the test is successful, then make the persistent change. If your platform supports it, use netplan try or configure a short rollback timer in your remote management tools. Keep a recovery plan such as console access or an out-of-band connector before restarting networking services. A concrete sequence: check interfaces, add a temporary IP with ip addr add, verify ping to gateway and a known host, then convert the settings into an ifcfg file or Netplan YAML and restart the service. Common misconception: a single command will always succeed; in practice network services and renderers may conflict. After changes, always verify with ip addr show, ip route show, and ping to confirm that both local and external connectivity behave as expected. Safe workflow for editing network config on remote servers means test changes incrementally, keep a rollback plan, and verify after applying persistent configuration to protect remote access.. In practical terms, plan, test, and verify to avoid accidental lockout. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Network interface bonding (teaming)
screens.narratorSegment: Bonding, sometimes called teaming or link aggregation, combines multiple physical interfaces into one logical interface so the system has resilience or greater throughput. The simplest benefit is redundancy: in active-backup mode, one slave carries traffic while the other waits; if the active link fails, traffic moves to the backup automatically. Another use is distributing traffic across links for higher aggregate bandwidth. Bonding is configured by creating a bond master interface and attaching physical interfaces as slaves. For example, create a bond0 master with nmcli, set its mode to active-backup, then add slave connections for each physical interface and assign the bond IP address. After activation, ip addr show bond0 returns the single logical address, and physical failures are transparent to the IP layer. A common misconception is that bonding alone increases per-flow bandwidth; depending on the bonding mode and switch configuration, single flows may still be limited to one physical link. Always coordinate bonding mode with network switch settings and verify behavior with ip addr show and checking slave link states. How would you validate failover? Simulate a physical link down and watch the bond switch to the remaining slave.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Network interface bonding (teaming)
Concept

Bonding aggregates physical links into a single logical interface for redundancy or load distribution depending on mode.

Typical nmcli sequence
sudo nmcli connection add type bond con-name mybond0 ifname bond0 mode active-backup ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.150/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 autoconnect yes
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name bond0-slave-enp0s3 ifname enp0s3 master bond0
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name bond0-slave-enp0s8 ifname enp0s8 master bond0
sudo nmcli connection up mybond0
Practical checks
  • Confirm bond IP with ip addr show bond0.
  • Inspect slave states and link health with cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 or NetworkManager status.
  • Test failover by administratively bringing a slave down and observing continuity.
Misconception
Bonding does not automatically increase single-flow throughput unless the mode and switch support distribution across flows. Understand your traffic patterns when choosing a mode.
Key Takeaway

Use bonding to add resilience; pick modes thoughtfully and verify with failover tests and slave state inspection.

screens.title: Commands for common verification and troubleshooting

You will learn two complementary patterns: quick, temporary changes using the kernel tools for testing and troubleshooting, and persistent, reboot-surviving configuration using higher-level systems like NetworkManager or Netplan. We'll also cover distribution-specific file formats such as ifcfg scripts and Netplan YAML, and show how to create a bonded interface to increase availability or throughput. Throughout, you'll practice verification commands and learn common mistakes to avoid, such as wrong gateways or IP conflicts. A concrete example you will see is configuring a second interface with a static address using nmcli, then validating it with ip addr show and ping. By the end you will understand when to use a transient change for a quick test and when to commit a persistent configuration safely so the system retains settings after reboot. Keep in mind the safety rule for remote machines: always have a recovery channel before modifying primary network interfaces. Ready to explore temporary commands, persistent files, and resilient bonding? Let’s begin.

These objectives map the practical skills you will gain. First, you will be able to distinguish between temporary kernel-level changes and persistent configuration files or managers. That distinction matters because a quick test should not overwrite production settings. Second, you will configure static IP addresses, subnet masks, and default gateways from the command line so services and routing behave predictably. Third, you will manage NetworkManager-controlled systems using nmcli and nmtui, which lets you script changes or use a guided interactive interface. Finally, you will understand persistent formats — such as ifcfg scripts on Red Hat families and Netplan YAML on Ubuntu — and know how to apply those changes and restart services safely. Each objective includes procedures and verification commands so you can confirm connectivity. By the end of this chapter you should confidently move between temporary tests and durable configurations while avoiding common mistakes that cause lockout or IP conflicts.

These objectives translate directly to hands-on outcomes. You will identify interfaces with ip addr show and ip route show and interpret the output to decide addressing and routing changes. You will perform immediate tests with ip addr add, ip link set up or down, and ip route add to temporarily change connectivity without altering boot configuration. You will create, modify, and activate NetworkManager connections using nmcli for scripting and nmcli or nmtui for interactive edits, and know how to bring changes up with nmcli connection up. On systems that use Netplan, you will author a YAML file to set addresses, gateway, and nameservers then apply it with netplan apply. On Red Hat derived systems, you will edit ifcfg files and restart the appropriate network service to commit changes. Finally, you'll assemble a simple bond and attach two slave interfaces to achieve basic active-backup redundancy. These outcomes help you practice safe changes, verify connectivity, and avoid lockout on remote servers.

The ip command is the modern, supported tool for temporary network changes and inspection. Use it to add or remove addresses, bring interfaces up or down, and manipulate routes. In practice perform temporary changes incrementally and test connectivity at each step; if the test succeeds and you intend to keep the settings, translate the same values into your persistent method rather than relying on ip to survive reboots.
